en: Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Fifteen, Part Two: The Great Goddess of Eloquence.
Volume Eight: The Remainder of the "Chapter on the Great Goddess of Eloquence."
Sūtra: At that time, the Brahmin Kauṇḍinya, having spoken the aforementioned praises and the dhāraṇī-praise for the Goddess Sarasvatī, [the sūtra] proceeds to the fourth section:
Kauṇḍinya’s instruction on requesting her empowerment.
Regarding the previously requested method for attaining eloquence (*pratibhāna*), this request is now granted through empowerment.
It is divided into four main parts:

first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of what follows; second, the formal teaching of the request for empowerment, beginning with "Namo"; third, the praise and exhortation to practice by the goddess, beginning with "At that time, eloquence..."; and fourth, Cunda’s joyful acceptance and veneration.
The introduction has two parts;
this is the first, which concludes the preceding section.
The Sūtra says: [The Buddha] addressed the great assembly:

"O virtuous ones, if you wish to entreat the Goddess Sarasvatī to compassionately bestow her protection, so that in this present life you may attain unimpeded eloquence, brilliant great wisdom, and skillful speech; and so that you may master rare talents, and achieve in accordance with your will the adornment of discourse and composition without doubt or obstruction—[then do so]."
After descending to be born, there are three parts:
first, the announcement to the assembly; second, from "O virtuous ones" onwards, the specification of what is sought; and third, from "you should" onwards, the formal request for birth.
Within the section on the dharmas sought, the first part generally presents the four types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Clever" (*cōng*) refers to the capacity for comprehension; "clear" (*míng*) refers to the capacity for awakening; and "wisdom" (*zhì*) refers to the capacity for decisive resolution.
From "skillful and subtle" (*qiǎojiào*) onwards, the four types of eloquence are presented individually:
Skillfulness is the absence of impediment regarding words;
broad and comprehensive mastery is the absence of impediment regarding the meaning of the Dharma;
and the adornment of discourse is the absence of impediment regarding eloquence.
Sūtra: “One should thus invoke with utmost sincerity and reverence, saying:
[The following sections are as in the text]. Sūtra: “Namo buddhāya, namo dharmāya, namaḥ saṃghāya.”
"Homage to the assembly of all Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all noble sages.
Regarding the request for empowerment through the True Teaching, there are two parts:

first, the request for the Buddha’s empowerment so that [the goal] may be attained; second, from "Homage to the Buddhas’ Wondrous Eloquence" onwards, the request for the empowerment of Sarasvatī and others so that it may be attained.
The first part further consists of three sections:

first, the homage to the Triple Gem; second, the praise of the Buddha’s words and so forth as the basis for the request; and third, from "Homage, homage" onwards, the formal request for the World-Honored One’s empowerment so that [the goal] may be attained.
This is the first [section].

The Sūtra states: “All Buddhas of the past, present, and the ten directions have already practiced truthful speech; they are able to speak words that accord with the capacities of beings and are true, without any falsehood or deception. Having constantly spoken truthful words throughout immeasurable koṭis of great kalpas, they rejoice in all who possess truthful speech.”
The passage beginning with "Praising the Buddha’s words" and so forth serves as the introduction to the request.
First, the true speech is praised; next, the excellence of his speech is praised; finally, its benefit is praised.
There are three ways in which his speech is praised:
First, the cause is praised; next, from "Having already... onwards, the fruit is praised; and finally, from "Those who speak truthful words... onwards, sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is praised.
This clarifies that the World-Honored One and others possess immeasurable joy, which is attained through the absence of envy; therefore, he requests their empowerment.

Sūtra: “Because he does not speak falsely, he extends his broad and long tongue so that it can cover his face, cover Jambudvīpa and the four continents, cover a thousand, two thousand, and three thousand worlds, and universally cover the worlds of the ten directions, completely and pervasively in an inconceivable manner.”
The following section consists of words of praise.
The initial portion praises the cause by virtue of his truthfulness; from "extending his broad and long tongue" onwards, it praises the fruit.
The intention here is that since the Buddha’s speech causes one to seek [the goal] and ensures its certain attainment without falsehood, I now offer this request.
The Sūtra states: "It can eliminate the burning heat of all afflictions.
This is a praise of its benefits.
Because it is capable of providing such benefit, one requests the bestowal of empowerment, wishing to attain what the Buddha has attained.
Because of paying homage to the Triple Gem and because of seeking the equipment of speech, one respectfully pays homage by repeating the words.
According to all that is to be distinguished below, it is wished that everything be attained.
Because the Buddha is supreme and is the root, he is specifically requested first.

Sūtra: “I pay homage, I pay homage to all Buddhas. May I, [Name], likewise attain the accomplishment of subtle and wondrous eloquence. With a sincere heart, I take refuge in and pay homage to the wondrous eloquence of all Buddhas, the wondrous eloquence of the great Bodhisattvas, the wondrous eloquence of the noble Pratyekabuddhas, the wondrous eloquence of those on the four paths and four fruits, the wondrous eloquence of the speech of the Four Noble Truths, and the wondrous eloquence of right practice and right view.”
Next, the request for the deities such as Mañjuśrī to bestow their empowerment so that [the goal] may be attained.
This section has two parts:
first, prostrating to the sought-after Mañjuśrī; second, from "I pay homage to the non-deceptive one" onwards, requesting their empowerment so that [the goal] may be attained.

Regarding the initial section on "Paying Homage to the Object of Seeking," first, the two characters "pay homage" (*namas*) identify the one who pays homage; second, the twenty-two categories beginning with "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*) distinguish the objects of worship and seeking; and third, the passage beginning with "all supreme activities" requests that those who can accomplish these grant me the necessary resources to attain them.
Of the six verses, the first one and a half concern the eloquence of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), while the remainder concerns the eloquence of other devas and ṛṣis.
Within the section on the Noble Ones, the first verse identifies the person capable of achieving it;
the subsequent half-verse clarifies the nature of what is expounded, briefly citing three categories as illustrations for all phenomena (*dharma*).
There are six kinds of correct practice:
first, the most excellent correct practice; second, mental attention; third, conformity with the Dharma; fourth, avoiding the two extremes; fifth, differentiation; and sixth, non-differentiation.

Regarding the correct practice based on the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), each has its own six types of correct practice, as explained in the third chapter of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*.

There are eleven types of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*): viewing the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) as being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, and like an obstruction; viewing it through the eight aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; viewing the origin (*samudaya*) as a fetter; viewing cessation (*nirodha*) as liberation from bonds; and viewing the path (*mārga*) as that which enables liberation from bonds—these added to the previous ones make eleven.

Sūtra: “The wondrous eloquence of the Brahma-multitude seers; the wondrous eloquence of Mahādeva and Umā; the wondrous eloquence of Skandadeva; the wondrous eloquence of King Mānasvin; the wondrous eloquence of the intelligent Rātridevī; the wondrous eloquence of the Four Great Kings; the wondrous eloquence of the son of heaven Sunirmita; the wondrous eloquence of Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets; the wondrous eloquence of Vaiśravaṇa; the wondrous eloquence of the goddess Viśvamātṛ; the wondrous eloquence of the deity Śiṣya; the wondrous eloquence of the goddess Śrī; the wondrous eloquence of Śvetaketu; the wondrous eloquence of the speech of Hārītī; the wondrous eloquence of the Mothers and Great Mothers; the wondrous eloquence of the Mother Hārītī; the wondrous eloquence of the various yakṣas; and the wondrous eloquence of the kings of the ten directions.”
The remainder below [the Brahmakāyika heaven] consists of the Brahmakāyikas, who are themselves ṛṣis because they are free from desire;
or else, the Brahmakāyikas and the ṛṣis are distinct.
The first interpretation is correct.
Regarding Mahādeva and Umā: this refers to Umā, the name of the consort of Maheśvara (Mahādeva) in the desire realm.
"Umā" means "to stop. Because her father, Mahādeva, stopped her when she wished to marry and did not permit it, she is called "Mahādeva-stops" (Mahādeva-umā).
*Saṃskṛta* means "aggregate" (*skandha*) in this context; in the West, the intestines, shoulders, and so forth are called *skandhas*, because they are accumulations of matter.
*Manas* means "compassionate mind" (*maitracitta*).
Vaiśravaṇa means "many hands" in this language; it is an alternative name for the deity Nārāyaṇa.
Vi means "various" and ma means "karma"; this is what was formerly called Vaiśravaṇa (or Viśvakarman).
The deities who serve [the Buddha] include Śrī, which is translated here as "Auspiciousness" (Jixiang);
Śrīmātā, which is translated here as "Auspicious Wisdom" (Jixianghui);
and Heḷi, for which there is no equivalent translation.
*Hariti* means "blue" in this [language]. Following the scripture:
"May all supreme karmic merit assist me, enabling me to practice inexhaustible and wondrous eloquence," one requests that [the Buddhas] bestow their empowerment so that this may be attained.

Sūtra: “Homage to the one who is without deception; homage to the one who is liberated; homage to the one who has transcended desire; homage to the one who has abandoned the hindrances and coverings; homage to the one whose mind is pure; homage to the one who is luminous; homage to the one who speaks the truth; homage to the one who is free from the habit-energies of dust; homage to the one who abides in the ultimate truth; homage to the Lord of the Great Assembly.”
The final twenty-five verses constitute the request for empowerment so that [the goal] may be attained.

This is divided into seven sections: first, twelve verses of homage and salutation to the Bodhisattvas requesting their empowerment; second, one and a half verses requesting the empowerment of the Śrāvakas; third, two and a half verses requesting the empowerment of the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); fourth, two verses requesting the empowerment of the gods of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); fifth, five verses requesting the empowerment of the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭanikāya*); sixth, one verse requesting the empowerment of other humans and devas; and seventh, one verse requesting the empowerment of all sentient beings within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The first part consists of three sections.

The first seven verses request empowerment to attain the eloquence of a bodhisattva; the next three verses request empowerment to attain the eloquence of a Tathāgata; and the final two verses request empowerment to attain the eloquence of Buddhas, śrāvakas, and others.
The beginning and middle sections further consist of two parts:

the first two and a half verses generally pay homage to all bodhisattvas and request their empowerment; the subsequent four and a half verses specifically pay homage to the goddesses and request their empowerment.
This is the initial general summary.
It praises and pays homage to ten virtues:
first, the virtue of being free from pride and devoid of deception;
Second, the virtue of realizing true analytical cessation, which is distinct from that of the two vehicles;
third, the virtue of being unstained by the five sensory objects;
fourth, the virtue of being able to abandon the entanglements and hindrances; and—
Fifth, the virtue of constant activity free from outflows;
sixth, the virtue of destroying ignorance and generating wisdom;
seventh, the virtue of speech that necessarily accords with its object.
Eighth, the virtue of being free from all habitual tendencies;
ninth, the virtue of spontaneously realizing the truth;
tenth, the virtue of guiding sentient beings.
The ten phrases of the sutra text are explained and correlated in their respective order.

Sutra: “I pay homage to the Goddess of Eloquence; may my speech be unimpeded. May all that I seek be swiftly accomplished; may I be free from illness and always abide in peace. May my lifespan be extended; may I skillfully understand all vidyā-mantras. May I diligently cultivate the path to Bodhi, extensively benefiting all sentient beings, and may my heart’s wishes be fulfilled early.”
I speak words of truth; I speak words free from deception. O Goddess of Celestial Eloquence, grant me accomplishment.
I pray that you, O Goddess, will come, so that my speech may be without impediment; enter swiftly into my body and mouth, and grant me wisdom and abundant eloquence.
The section on separately requesting the celestial maidens is divided into five parts;
the first is the unimpeded words of request.
The second section consists of one verse requesting freedom from illness and longevity, so as not to cling to worldly life for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
the third section consists of one verse requesting the elucidation of secret mantras and diligent practice toward bodhicitta;
the fourth section consists of one verse clarifying that one truly requests empowerment to attain these goals.
The fifth section, consisting of one verse, requests the goddess to enter the body and bestow her blessings.
From the Sūtra: "May my tongue-root obtain the eloquence of the Tathāgata; through the power of that speech, may all sentient beings be tamed."
When I speak, my words accord with reality and are always successful; those who hear them develop reverence, and what I do is never in vain.
If I seek eloquence, [may it be granted].
If the matter were not accomplished,
the truthful words of the goddess would all become false.
The request for the Tathāgata to explain is divided into three parts;
the first two lines constitute the request.
The next one and a half verses clarify the intention for seeking discernment;
the following verse establishes the contrary: the words of the Celestial One are not in vain, and my seeking shall surely succeed. Sūtra:

“For those who have committed the crimes of immediate retribution, the Buddha’s words bring them to discipline; likewise, for the Arhats and all those who speak of repaying kindness—Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, the foremost among the World-Honored One’s assembly—their words are true and real. May I achieve all such accomplishments.”
The following requests for empowerment so that the Buddha and his śrāvakas may attain eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
The first half-verse requests the Buddha’s eloquence; the one and a half verses request the eloquence of the others.
"Buddha-tamed" refers to uninterrupted speech.
"Arhat" is a term for repaying kindness;
it serves as a mutual illustration for all such expressions.
As for the phrase "these [beings]," it may refer equally to other Arhats, or it may refer equally to the twenty-two types of persons previously distinguished.
Sūtra: “I now summon and invite the assembly of the Buddha’s śrāvakas; may you all swiftly arrive and fulfill my heart’s aspiration.
Regarding the true words I seek, may they all be without falsehood.”
[He] uttered this invocation to summon the śrāvakas.

The Sūtra says: "From Akaniṣṭha above, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities, Mahābrahmā and the Brahmakāyika gods, the entire host of Brahma-kings, extending even throughout the trichiliocosm to the Lord of the Sahā World and his retinue—I now summon them all; I pray that you will descend with compassion and, out of pity, accept me together."
Next, he requested the deities of the Form Realm to provide their empowerment.

The Sūtra says: “The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the hosts of the Tuṣita Heaven where Maitreya shall become a Buddha; the Yāma devas, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the hosts of the Caturmahārājika Heaven, and all the various hosts of devas.”
Next, the request for the deities of the desire realm to bestow their empowerment is given in the Sūtra:

“The deities of earth, water, fire, and wind who dwell upon Mount Sumeru; the hosts of deities of the seven seas and mountains, together with all their retinues; Pūrṇabhadraka and the Five-Crested One; the sun, moon, and all the constellations—may all such assemblies of devas bring peace and security to the world.”
These various celestial deities do not delight in committing sinful deeds.

I pay homage to the Mother of Ghosts and her youngest beloved son, as well as the hosts of nāgas, devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and mahoragas. By the power of the World-Honored One, I summon you all; I pray that you will descend with a heart of compassion and grant me unimpeded eloquence.
Next, he requests the empowerment of the eight classes of beings; the first four verses state their names, and the final verse is the formal request.
The Sūtra says: “All you multitudes of humans and devas who are able to know the minds of others, may you all grant your divine power and bestow upon me wondrous eloquence.”
"Even unto the end of empty space, pervading the entire dharma-realm, may all classes of sentient beings be granted to me wondrous eloquence.
This is the prayer for others—gods, humans, and all beings within the dharma-realm.
Sūtra: At that time, having heard this request, the Goddess of Eloquence addressed the Brahmin, saying:
“Excellent, Great Being!

If there are men or women who, according to the aforementioned ritual for upholding [this practice], rely upon these mantras and mantra-praises, take refuge in and revere the Triple Gem with a devout mind and right mindfulness, then whatever they seek shall not be in vain. Furthermore, if they also uphold, read, and recite this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra, then whatever they wish to attain will surely be fulfilled and quickly accomplished, except in cases where they lack a sincere heart.”
At that time, the brahmin was filled with deep joy in his heart; he joined his palms and received [the teaching] upon the crown of his head.
Next, the third goddess exhorted him to practice, which is twofold:

First, the goddess offers praise; next, from "If there is a man" onwards, she seals [the teaching] and exhorts him to practice; finally, from "At that time, the brahmin" onwards, Caturāśva expresses his joy and receives [the teaching].
Sūtra: At that time, the Buddha addressed the goddess Prajñākūṭā:
“Excellent, excellent, O virtuous goddess!

"You are able to propagate this sovereign king of subtle sūtras, to protect all who uphold it, and to benefit all sentient beings, enabling them to attain peace and happiness. By preaching such a Dharma, you bestow inconceivable eloquence and obtain immeasurable merit; all who resolve their minds [for enlightenment] shall swiftly proceed toward Bodhi."
The third major section of the lower grade: The Tathāgata’s Praise and Exhortation. First, he praises the goddess;
from "All who have resolved their minds" (*sarva-cittotpādika*) onwards, he exhorts them to rely upon and practice the teachings.
Chapter Sixteen: The Chapter on the Great Auspicious Goddess (end of Part Five). The Chapter on the Great Auspicious Goddess, Chapter Sixteen, is analyzed according to three sections:
First, the intent; second, the explanation of the name; third, the resolution of difficulties.
Regarding the intent: there are five aspects to the practice and circulation [of this teaching];
here, it causes one to cultivate merit and wisdom, specifically providing the second [aspect], which is the giving of clothing and material wealth.

If there were no benefit or merit, one might fear that external seeking would hinder the propagation of the sutra; therefore, it is taught that while practicing and studying according to the sutra, one naturally obtains clothing and other necessities.
Since the affliction of seeking from without is eliminated, one is further able to cultivate merit and wisdom to accomplish these sublime practices; for this reason, this chapter follows.

Regarding the explanation of the names: *Mahā* in Sanskrit means "Great" (*da* in Chinese); *Śrī* means "Auspiciousness" (*jíxiáng* in Chinese); *Devī* means "Heavenly Maiden" (*tiānnǚ* in Chinese). The collective name is thus "The Great Auspicious Heavenly Maiden."
This chapter explains the matters concerning that goddess Śrī; therefore, it is named accordingly.

Regarding the resolution of difficulties: the preceding chapter benefited her eloquence, while the subsequent chapter benefits her food and drink; in both cases, they were not separately divided into distinct chapters.
Regarding these additional robes, why should they not be divided separately? Answer:

They should not be divided separately, as the preceding and succeeding cases correspond to one another; however, because there are differences in detail and brevity, the manner of opening and closing [the categories] varies.

The preceding chapter briefly clarifies the benefits of seeking [the Dharma], but as the text is concise, it could not be treated separately and was thus explained in conjunction with the text on seeking and discerning;

the subsequent chapter on propagating the sutra involves increasing the essence of the earth, yet it does not state that this is added only after one has finished seeking, and therefore it too was not treated separately.
This benefit concerns clothing; although the initial heading concerning the benefit of clothing was broad and extensive, it is now divided into two [chapters].
Question:
Since both [the Bodhisattvas] equally benefit the propagation of the sutra, why is it that their eloquence and robes only increase after being specifically requested,
whereas in the subsequent chapter, the flavor of the earth increases without waiting for a request and is obtained immediately?
Answer: Transformations have myriad paths, and their principles do not conform to a single standard.
Furthermore, it is difficult to obtain clothing through seeking, whereas it is easy to increase the flavor of the earth; therefore, [the former] does not depend on seeking.
Since the deity acts with autonomy, it is all the more easy [to succeed].
Question:
One who upholds this sutra should naturally provide all four requisites for offerings; why then must one seek them before increasing their wealth and resources?

Answer: One who practices the recitation of the sutras should naturally obtain the four requisites; however, because one wishes to bring about meritorious conduct, one further causes them to request [these requisites].
Moreover, those who exclusively propagate the sutras do not yet seek these four requisites.
Because she was made to practice the sutra for the sake of those seeking the four requisites, he waited until she had studied and sought them according to the sutra before granting them.
Question:
To which realm does this auspicious woman belong?
"Is it the realm of hungry ghosts? Answer:
The Tripitaka Master Zhenti said:
"This Bodhisattva of the first stage should become a tree deity king (*vṛkṣadeva-rāja*), leading all the deities to wherever he goes to bestow supreme bliss upon others.
Since this supreme bliss is the fruit of merit, she is named Puṇyavatī (Goddess of Merit)."
"In foreign lands, spirits are also called devas.
Based on this interpretation, it indicates that he is a king among the tree-spirits within the realm of hungry ghosts.
Now, [I] shall explain:
According to the sutras, these are merely called "celestial maidens" (devakanyā) and are not described as "spirits" (deva), for it is only those of the lower realms who are designated as "spirits.

Even where they are referred to as "tree-spirit kings," this is analogous to how the Four Heavenly Kings are also called "Four Heavenly Spirit Kings"; they are termed "spirit kings" because they preside over spirits, yet this does not necessarily mean they belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
The goddesses are likewise; they are included within the celestial realm (*devagati*).
The Sūtra says: At that time, the Great Auspicious Goddess rose from her seat, went before the Buddha to prostrate at his feet, joined her palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If I should see any bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā who receives, maintains, recites, and explains this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* to others, I shall single-mindedly pay respectful homage and provide offerings to these Dharma-preachers—namely, food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and all other necessary requisites—ensuring they are fully provided for and lack nothing.
The commentary states:

"Dividing the distribution of material goods into two parts, this first chapter clarifies that those who propagate the sutra should receive four requisites; the subsequent chapter clarifies the method for obtaining them."
The first part is divided into four sections:
first, seeing those who propagate the sutra, one is able to provide them with the four requisites;
second, from "World-Honored One" onwards, it distinguishes the causes for being able to make offerings, as well as the repayment of their virtue.
3. From "If again" onwards, there is the exhortation to practice and study;
4. From "The Buddha told" onwards, the Buddha praises and exhorts toward accomplishment.
This is the first [section].
This is further divided into three parts:
first, the ritual of requesting instruction; second, from "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, the vision of practice; and third, from "I shall" onwards, the bestowing of benefit.
There are two types of benefit:
first, the worldly benefit; second, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, they shall also encounter... onwards, the supramundane benefit.
There are two kinds of worldly benefit:
The first provides benefit in the present; the section beginning with "Furthermore" below provides benefit for the future.
Within the present benefit, the first provides material wealth.

The Sūtra says: "Whether by day or by night, one should dwell in peace by observing and contemplating all the words and meanings of this King of Sūtras, so that this scripture may be widely circulated throughout Jambudvīpa, ensuring that those sentient beings who have planted roots of goodness under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas may always hear it and that it does not quickly disappear."
"Next, he bestows the benefit of the Dharma.
There are two aspects to this benefit of the Dharma:
first, it enables those who practice the Dharma to dwell in peace and happiness;"
Second, to ensure that the teaching flows for a long time, there are three parts:
first, causing the Dharma to abide for a long duration; second, identifying the causes for its faithful acceptance; and third, ensuring it is constantly heard and does not perish.

Sūtra: "Furthermore, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, they shall experience various superior joys among devas and humans; harvests shall always be abundant, famine shall be forever eliminated, and all sentient beings shall constantly enjoy peace and happiness."
Regarding the subsequent benefits, there are three:

first, attaining a superior body; second, "always obtaining abundant harvests" and below, which refers to constant abundance and joy; third, "all sentient beings" and below, which refers to the ability to benefit others.

Sūtra: “Furthermore, you shall encounter various Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and in a future age, swiftly realize the fruit of unsurpassed, great Bodhi, forever severing the suffering and hardships of the cycle of rebirth within the three miserable realms.”
Next, there are three types of supramundane benefits:
first, encountering a Buddha; second, attaining bodhi; and third, "permanently severing the three miserable realms" and subsequently realizing nirvana.
Sūtra: “World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past there was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Vaidūrya-Golden-Mountain-Jewel-Flower-Radiance-Illuminating-Auspicious-Virtue-Ocean, fully endowed with the ten titles.”

Regarding the roots of goodness I have planted there, through the compassionate mindfulness and the majestic spiritual power of that Tathāgata, may I today—in whatever place I think of, in whatever direction I look, and in whatever country I arrive—be able to cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings to experience all manner of happiness; and furthermore, may they be fully provided with all necessities such as clothing, food and drink, and the requisites for life, as well as treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and pearls.
The following section distinguishes the causes for being able to make offerings and serves as a report on his merits;
it has four parts:
first, recounting his past encounter with the Buddha.
2. From "I [at]" below, it describes the causes planted in the past;
3. From "By means of that" below, it reflects upon the grace of that Buddha;

4. From "Causing me" below, it indicates that I am able to benefit others, that I act to repay the grace of the Buddhas of the past, and that I make offerings to and benefit those who propagate the sutra.
The Buddha praised him, saying,
"You are able to thus recollect past causes and offer worship in gratitude," and so forth.
This corresponds to the object of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (paracittajñāna), which follows whatever is being recollected.
In whichever direction one looks, that which is seen is through the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*).
To whichever place one goes, that which is reached is through the supernormal power of the miraculous domain (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-abhijñā*).
Regarding the eight treasures herein, others mostly speak of seven; moreover, the locations where these seven treasures are described also differ.
In accordance with the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which states, "The seven [offerings] are taught differently according to what is valued in various regions," there is thus no contradiction.

Furthermore, if anyone should read and recite this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* with a sincere heart, they should also daily burn various famous incenses and exquisite flowers as an offering for me to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnavairocanaśrīguṇasāgara of the Lapis Lazuli Golden Mountain. Moreover, they should daily invoke my name during the three periods of the day and separately offer me incense, flowers, and various fine foods; by also hearing and receiving this wondrous King of Sūtras, they shall obtain such merit.
The following passage encourages the practice of training.
According to Paramārtha’s interpretation, the former [verse] benefits the Dharma teacher, while this one benefits the listener;
however, my current intention applies to both.
First is the prose exposition, followed by the verse hymn.
The prose exposition consists of five parts:
first, the exhortation to read and recite it oneself;
2. From "Also should" (*yi dang*) below, he teaches the ritual for recitation;

Alternatively, because the deity is able to make the ground firm, she is named the Deity of the Firm Ground; this is also an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative compound), as the ability to make the ground firm is the function of the deity.

Sūtra: "This causal condition is what the Buddha has personally realized: 'I know all dharmas; I understand all dharmas, according to all that exists as dharmas and as each dharma exists—the distinctions in the categories and essential natures of all dharmas.'"
The subsequent explanation has two parts:

The first part clarifies the two types of wisdom that are capable of knowing; the section beginning with "according to what exists" clarifies the phenomena that are known.
"Knowing" refers to subsequent cognition (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), while "realizing" refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). "Being enlightened" means thorough comprehension.
"According to what exists" means according to all types of merit that exist;
this is the nature of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
"As it exists" refers to all the principles of how things exist; this is the nature of existence as it is (*yathāvadbhāvatā*).
The former refers to the substantial entities of phenomena (*dharmas*), while the latter refers to the principles of phenomena.
The former refers to the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the latter refers to the phenomena of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the nature as it is (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*) is spoken of as suchness (*tathatā*) alone from the perspective of the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-bhāva*).
These correspond respectively to the objects of the two aforementioned types of knowledge.
The preceding section specifically clarifies the dharmas that are known, while the passage beginning with "the categories of all dharmas" generally clarifies all dharmas that are known.
If conventional phenomena possess many types of distinctions in their essential natures,

although ultimate reality lacks such distinctions in its essential nature— being the true nature of those very phenomena— it is nevertheless said that the supported meaning also possesses distinctions in accordance with its supports.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma*, "as far as it extends" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) refers to the aggregates, bases, and elements;
"as it is" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) refers to the Four Truths, the sixteen aspects, and so forth; thus, there is a distinction between them.

Chapter Twenty: The Righteous Discourse on the King’s Dharma (end of Section Five). The "Righteous Discourse on the King’s Dharma" is analyzed according to three gates.
Regarding the intent of this discourse, there are three aspects to its circulation:

first, within the "Circulation of Study and Practice" consisting of the initial sixteen chapters, there are five sections; this is the third chapter, which explicitly clarifies the upholding and study [of the precepts].
There are two aspects to upholding the training:
the first two cite the past, and the last one exhorts the present.
Within citing the past, there are two parts:
The first is the path for higher rebirth (*abhyudaya-mārga*), and the second is the path for definitive excellence (*niḥśreyasa-mārga*).
This chapter concerns the former. Furthermore, another interpretation states:

According to the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings Protecting the Nation," if a human king can honor people and revere the Dharma, correctly practicing and propagating the sutras, then the devas and others will protect him;
if he does not do so, the devas and others will abandon him.
Therefore, this present chapter is presented to exhort the assembly by citing how a king of the past correctly practiced and propagated the sutra; thus, this chapter arises.
As for the explanation of the chapter title, one first analyzes the terms separately and then combines them.
The King has three titles:
the first is Huang; Huang means the Heavenly King.
The second is Di; Di means the Sovereign.
The third is called *rāja*. "King" (*rāja*) means "to return to" (*ni*), for he is one to whom the multitude returns;
he is also generally termed a "lord" (*juna*).
Furthermore, one who exercises sovereign authority and autonomy is named a king.
"Dharma" refers to a rule or standard.
"Right" (samyak) serves to distinguish it from the wrong; it is also termed "noble" (ārya).

For example, within the context of loving speech, one gives rise to the four pure speeches and the eight noble speeches. Pure speech refers to the absence of false speech and so forth; noble speech refers to saying "I have seen" when one has indeed seen, and so on.
"Discourse" (śāstra) refers to definitive analysis (*viniścaya*), which involves the repeated investigation and examination of the principles of all phenomena (*dharma*).
A "king" is one who is able to practice the Dharma.
"The Dharma of Right Discourse" is precisely the Dharma that is practiced.
It should be called the *Rājadharma-samyak-śāstra*. Following the Indian linguistic convention, it is called the *Dharmasamyak-śāstra*.
In this title, "śāstra" (treatise) is the agent of discourse (*abhidheya*), while "right dharma" (*samyak-dharma*) is the object of discourse (*abhidheya*).
Both "the king’s right dharma" and "the treatise on right dharma" are analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Now, this treatise correctly elucidates the King’s True Dharma; it does not intend to provide separate expositions on the King or the Treatise on the True Dharma.
Regarding the resolution of objections, a question is raised:
When the Earth Deity requested the Buddha to preach the King’s True Dharma, why did he not himself explain the matters concerning the abiding state?
Answer: It is because he wishes to clarify that the dharmas of the three periods of time are all identical.
Since the Dharma is most venerable and supreme, he does not speak of it personally, but merely cites past events.
Question:

Since governing a kingdom relies on conventional worldly affairs, the words spoken by the past Brahmā King are cited here.
In reality, the Brahmā King himself heard them from the Buddha and then spoke them to the Four Great Kings.
As was the case when Sujāta heard the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* from Ratnakūṭa, it did not say that the Buddha had spoken it.
