The Sūtra states: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā in the midst of the great assembly, saying:
"You should listen attentively."
In the past, there was a king named Baladhvaja. That king had a son named Sudhvaja, who had not long been consecrated to the position of crown prince.
At that time, the father king said to Sudhvaja:

"There is a treatise on the true dharma of kings called the *Devendrasamaya-nīti*. In the past, when I was consecrated as the sovereign of the land, my father king, named Jñānabaladhvaja, expounded this treatise on the true dharma of kings for me."
Relying upon this treatise, I have governed the realm well for twenty thousand years; I do not recall ever having entertained a single thought of acting contrary to the Dharma.
You, too, should act likewise today; do not govern the kingdom through unrighteous means.
"What is called the Right Treatise on Royal Law?
Listen well now, and I shall explain it to you.
Next, the World-Honored One spoke for him; therein are three parts:

First, he issues a command to the assembly to listen; next, from "In the past" onwards, he recounts the former origins; finally, from "At that time, the Honored One of Power" onwards, he sets forth the former True Dharma.
The account of the past causal origins consists of eight parts:
first, the teacher and the recipient of the teaching;
second, from "At that time" onwards, the elucidation of the Dharma bestowed.

The "Lord of the World" is none other than the Brahmā King; it is only by cultivating the four immeasurables that one becomes a Lord of the World. It is clear that through teaching, compassion, and the arousal [of these states], one is certainly able to extract suffering and bestow happiness.
Third, from "I, at... onwards, the conditions for attaining the Dharma are explained.
4. From "My father" onwards, it clarifies the place where the Dharma was heard.
5. From "I rely upon" onwards, it clarifies my ability to practice and study.
6. From "You, now" onwards, it admonishes the son to follow and cultivate [the teachings].
7. From "What is it called... onwards, [the Buddha] hears the command and requests instruction.
8. From "You now... onwards, he issues the command to grant permission for the teaching.

The meaning of this is that because the son heard it from his father and was further instructed by him, it clarifies that the bond between father and son is profound and that the instruction will surely bring real benefit; therefore, he exhorts the listeners to revere and rely upon its practice.
Sūtra: “At that time, King Baladharaketu addressed his son with a sublime gāthā, expounding the True Discourse, as follows:
Below this, the ancient True Dharma is set forth.
The text is divided into two parts;
this is the introductory heading of the Buddha.
The Sūtra says: "I shall expound the Treatise on Royal Law to benefit and bring peace to all sentient beings, to sever the doubts of the world, and to eliminate all faults."
"All you kings of the devas and kings among men, should give rise to a heart of joy and listen to my words with palms joined.
Thus he spoke, and the following exposition consists of seventy-three verses, divided into two parts:
the first two verses command the powerful ones to listen, and the subsequent seventy-one verses present the formal discourse.

In the "Command to Listen" section, the first line describes the benefit of the discourse; the next three lines set forth what the teaching encompasses; and the final line commands one to listen so that it may be explained.
Question:
In the preceding prose section, it was stated that [the teaching] was only for the sake of his son; why, then, does this command to listen further include celestial beings and human kings?
Answer: The prose section is abbreviated because it is expanded upon in the verses. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
This is specifically for the purpose of admonishing you, my son.

My intention is that since this treatise accords with reason and brings vast benefit, both the Lord of Heaven and the King of Men shall rejoice; therefore, you should now listen with palms joined in reverence.
Sūtra: “In the past, the hosts of devas gathered on Vajra Mountain. The Four Kings rose from their seats and questioned Mahābrahmā:
‘O Lord Brahmā, Most Victorious One, Sovereign among the gods, we pray that you take pity upon us and sever all our doubts.’”
The following seventy-one verses present the formal argument (*siddhānta*).
This main section is divided into three parts:
the first two verses discuss the cause for the arising [of the treatise]; the next two verses introduce the inquiry; and the final sixty-seven verses present the formal argument itself.
The introduction consists of five parts:

the first two lines concern the place where the assembly has gathered; the next line concerns the person who makes the request; the next line concerns the subject of the inquiry; the next two lines praise that treatise; and the final two lines constitute the request for its exposition.
Sūtra: “How is it that one dwelling in the human world is named a ‘deva’?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is one called a ‘son of heaven’ (*devaputra*)?
How is it that, being born among humans, one alone attains the status of lord of men?”
"How is it that he dwells in the heavens and further becomes a Heavenly King?
Thus, four questions are raised in total, as can be seen from the text.
Each section contains three parts:

first, inquiring about their titles established based on virtue; this simultaneously includes inquiring about the reasons for establishing those titles, which refers to asking what kind of righteous dharma the kings practiced to earn names such as "King" and so forth.
If it were not so, the Four Heavenly Kings would have merely inquired after his name; why then would the Lord of Devas say, "I ask you about the methods for governing a kingdom"?
Thus, the *Sāṭhāgata-nirgrantha-sūtra*, fascicle two, states: "The King said:
'O Great Teacher!'"
"For what reason are those kings called 'kings'?
He replied:
"Great King!"
"A king is the parent of the people; because he is able to sustain and protect sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma, bringing them peace and happiness, he is called a 'king'.
This is the general statement.

Next, the commentary explains: "Great King, you should know that in nourishing the people, a king should treat them as his own infants; he should move them from dryness to moisture without waiting for their words. Why is this?..."

"Great King, you should know that a king establishes his reign by taking the people as his state; if the hearts of the people are not at peace, the state will perish. Therefore, a king must always concern himself for the people, never letting them depart from his mind, just as one thinks of an infant."

One should know the suffering and joy of the people within the realm, the floods, droughts, winds, and rains; their hunger and satiety, their youth and old age; their illnesses, legal disputes, and whether they are guilty or innocent, meritorious or lacking merit—one who knows these things in this way is said to be "not separated from the mind."

Having understood this, one should protect others through skillful means: providing at the proper time what ought to be given, reflecting with care upon what ought to be taken, employing laborers at the appropriate moment without depriving them of their interests, and restraining the greedy and violent so that people may attain peace and happiness.
"This is called protecting the nation; he is named a king.
The intent of this present dialogue is also the same as that.
The meaning of the third question is as follows:
By what karmic actions are those in the present and future born into the human world and receive names such as "deva"?
By what karmic actions are they born in the heavens and become celestial kings?
Therefore, the answer below states:
"By the power of prior virtuous karma, one is born in the heavens and attains the status of a king," and so forth.
According to the customs of Western countries, each object has ten names; here, three are cited for the human king and one for the celestial king, by way of illustration for the remainder.
Sūtra: “‘Thus do you protect the world?
Having thus questioned that Brahmā King, the Lord of the Brahmā Heaven then spoke to him: ‘O Protector of the World, you should know:
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, you have asked me about the methods of governing a kingdom; listen well as I explain them.’”
The following sixty-seven verses present the actual discourse. This section has three parts:

first, the two initial verses provide an introduction regarding the previous promise to speak; second, the next sixty verses constitute the actual discourse by the Lord of the Gods (Śakra); third, the final four and a half verses beginning with "Therefore, O King of Men" exhort [the listener] to rely upon and study [the teaching].
The first part is divided into two sections:
the first verse introduces the power of the Honored One, and the second verse records the Lord of Devas’ permission to speak and his exhortation to listen.
The Sūtra says: “By the power of past virtuous karma, one is born in heaven and becomes a king;”
"If one is among human beings, one shall rule as a sovereign.
Thus concludes the section on the Lord of Devas’ formal exposition, which consists of two parts:
the first three verses answer the two questions regarding his name and activities, thereby instructing him to cultivate goodness so as to create further causes for future rebirths.

Following the section "The Lord of the Thirty-three Gods," the subsequent fifty-seven and a half stanzas comprehensively answer the question regarding the reasons for attaining the title; they present the correct doctrine and instruct one to cultivate that which yields immediate benefit.
The first part further consists of two sections:
the first verse answers the latter two questions, while the subsequent two verses answer the former two questions.
This is the first [section].
Sūtra: "The various devas collectively bestow their protection, and only then does one enter the mother’s womb.
Once arrived within the womb, the various devas further provide guardianship.
Although born into the human world, one is called a 'deva' because of one's supreme excellence."
"Because he is protected by the devas, he is also called a 'Son of Heaven' (devaputra).
This response to the preceding questions consists of two parts:
the first one and a half verses answer the first question, and the latter half answers the second question.
Nevertheless, by virtue of the power of prior wholesome karma, this statement extends even to the gods who collectively provide protection. As the Sūtra says:

“The Lord of the Thirty-three Devas shares his power with the human king, and all the other devas likewise contribute their sovereign power to eliminate all that is contrary to the Dharma, to prevent evil karma from arising, and to instruct sentient beings in the cultivation of goodness so that they may be reborn in the heavens.”

Human beings, the hosts of asuras, gandharvas, and others, as well as rākṣasas and caṇḍālas—all provide half their strength, while parents provide the other half, causing them to abandon evil and cultivate goodness. The various devas collectively protect and sustain them, showing them the various rewards for good deeds;
yet if they commit various evil karmas, the devas will not protect them in this present life, showing them the various retributions for evil.
The following section provides a general response regarding the reasons for attaining the title [of Buddha] and presents the correct doctrine.
This text is further divided into two parts:
first, five verses that provide a brief outline; second, fifty-two and a half verses that offer a detailed explanation.
The section on the headings contains three parts;
the first two verses present the headings. Regarding the benefit to others through the various devas assisting the king in practicing the True Dharma, there are three points:
the first verse concerns the assistance of the devas, and the next verse concerns the king’s transformation of the world.
Within the section on transformation, the first half [of the verse] eliminates evil and the latter half generates goodness.
The subsequent one and a half verses indicate that humans and deities together provide protection for one's own benefit, or perhaps also for the benefit of others.

Through the assistance of human and divine powers, the King transforms others, causing them to abandon evil and cultivate goodness, so that together they may protect themselves and benefit one another.
As for the term "rākṣasa-caṇḍāla," *caṇḍāla* here means "one who bears fierce insignia and maintains evil ways"; it refers specifically to those among the rākṣasas who uphold such malevolence.
"If one protects even this evil mind, how much more so other virtuous ones?

The subsequent passage, beginning with "The devas protect them together," consists of one and a half verses that indicate how practicing virtue leads people to receive the protection of the devas; the first half-verse provides the general indication, while the following verse specifically shows the causes and effects obtained through good and evil.
Question:
It is possible to guard against the commission of wholesome deeds; how can one guard against the commission of unwholesome deeds? Answer:
Because he cultivated merit in the past, he has now attained the status of king; therefore, when people commit evil, the heavens manifest ill omens to protect him and cause him to reform his conduct.

As the Sūtra says: "If the people of the kingdom commit evil deeds and the king abandons them without restraint, this does not accord with correct principle; they should be governed and expelled according to the Dharma."
If one sees evil and does not restrain it, unrighteousness will flourish; consequently, within the king’s realm, deceit and fraud will increase day by day.
When the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three see that the people of the kingdom commit evil and the king fails to stop them, they all give rise to a mind of indignation.
Consequently, state administration is impaired and flattery and hypocrisy prevail in the world; they are invaded by hostile enemies and their territories are destroyed.
Their homes, possessions, and accumulated wealth are all lost, as various forms of deceit arise and people plunder one another.
Having attained kingship through the True Dharma, he fails to practice that Dharma; thus the people of the land are all dispersed and scattered, like an elephant trampling a lotus pond.
Malignant winds arise without constancy, torrential rains fall out of season, many strange and ominous stars appear, and the sun and moon are eclipsed, losing their light.
"The five grains, various flowers, and fruits—neither their sprouts nor their fruit will ripen; the land shall suffer famine because the king has abandoned the True Dharma.
Thus it is said. The following fifty-two and a half verses provide a detailed explanation, divided into two parts:

the first thirty-five verses clarify how calamities befall the king because he violates the True Dharma, while the latter seventeen and a half lines clarify how blessings befall the king because he relies upon the True Dharma.

In accordance with the sixty-first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Rājapraśāsti-śāstra*, the faults of a king, the virtues of a king, the gates of a king’s decline, the gates of a king’s skillful means, the qualities dear to a king, and the factors that can induce those qualities dear to a king are each presented through many categories, as explained extensively therein.
If one were to allocate these [terms] individually, the mode of analysis (*ākāra*) would be somewhat difficult.
Question:

This is titled *Rājanīti-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Correct Governance of Kings), and since its title corresponds to that of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*’s *Rājanīti-samyak-prakaraṇa*, why not rely on the latter for its explanation?
Answer: The principles do not follow a single path.

Texts such as the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Satyaka Nirgrantha-putra Sūtra* all clarify the methods for kings to practice governance; they are not identical in every detail, yet there is no contradiction in their respective applications.
Furthermore, based on this sūtra, the text is divided into two parts:

the first thirty lines extensively explain the arguments contradicting the correct doctrine, while the subsequent five verses beginning with "Thus, these boundless faults" conclude the refutation of the true Dharma.
The detailed explanation is divided into three parts:

first, eight verses clarify the fault of failing to prevent others from committing evil; second, nine verses beginning with "If the king abandons the True Dharma" clarify the fault of the king practicing what is contrary to the Dharma himself; and third, thirteen verses beginning with "The greatest minister in the land" clarify the fault of failing to eliminate the transgressions of ministers when they are seen.
The beginning and middle [of this section] further consist of four parts:

first, one verse clarifies that seeing evil should lead to its prevention; second, the verse beginning with "If one sees evil" clarifies the extensive non-prevention of evil; third, the section beginning with "When the king sees within his realm" explains how this provokes the wrath of the gods; fourth, the five verses beginning with "Because of this, state administration is impaired" show how calamities consequently arise.

There are five origins of calamity: first, when vengeful enemies destroy the state; second, when wealth is dispersed and mutual invasions occur; third, when disasters arise from their underlying causes; fourth, when portents and transformations appear simultaneously; and fifth, when the land suffers famine.
The five elements may be understood by correlating them with the sequence [of the text].
Within the third section on the causes of calamity, the first half provides the cause and the second half provides the analogy.
The Sūtra states: “If a king abandons the True Dharma and transforms people through evil laws, the various devas in their original palaces, having seen this, give rise to sorrow and distress.”
Those hosts of celestial kings spoke these words together:
"This king acts contrary to the Dharma; he associates with evil factions. His royal throne will not remain secure for long, and all the devas are filled with resentment."
"Because of that harboring of resentment, the kingdom shall fall into ruin.
Teaching people through unrighteousness will prevail within the land; strife and much deceit will arise, and epidemics will bring forth manifold sufferings."
The Lord of Devas will not protect him, and all other devas will abandon him; his kingdom shall perish, and the king’s body will suffer calamity and distress.
Both parents and wife and children, brothers and sisters alike, shall all undergo the pain of separation from those they love, even unto death.
Strange portents and falling meteors appeared; two suns rose simultaneously. Enemies and bandits from other lands arrived, and the people of the country suffered through calamity and disorder.
The high ministers whom the state esteemed died by violent and unjust means, and even the beloved elephants and horses were all lost and scattered.
"Arms and weapons shall prevail everywhere; many people shall die through unrighteousness; evil spirits shall enter the kingdom, and pestilence shall spread throughout.
This section, concerning the King’s own failure through his unrighteous conduct, is divided into four parts:

first, two lines clarifying that the King has abandoned the True Dharma; second, two lines showing how the devas perceive this and become sorrowful; third, two stanzas on the collective deliberation of the devas; fourth, six stanzas on the subsequent arising of calamities.
Within this, there are further nine [points]:
the first verse concerns the abundance of strife and the like;
the subsequent half-verse concerns the abandonment by the devas.
The next one and a half verses concern the arising of distressing events, the destruction of the realm, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
As for the king’s body undergoing suffering, this is precisely the suffering of association with the hated.
The separation from parents and others is the suffering of parting from what is loved (*priyaviprayoga-duḥkha*).
Up until the dissolution of the body is the suffering of death (*maraṇa-duḥkha*).
The subsequent half-verse describes the simultaneous arising of calamities and portents.
The first half-verse concerns the arrival of hostile bandits;
the next half-verse concerns the untimely death of high ministers;
and the following half-verse concerns the loss of livestock and property.
The latter half of the verse concerns the death of people through unrighteousness;
the subsequent half-verse concerns pestilence spreading throughout the land.
The Sūtra says: "The greatest ministers of the state, as well as all the auxiliary counselors, harbor flattery and sycophancy in their hearts, and all practice what is unrighteous."
"To see those who practice unrighteousness and yet feel love and respect for them;
while toward those who practice the Dharma, to treat them with harshness and inflict punishment.
The following thirteen verses concern the failure to eliminate faults committed by ministers; they are divided into four parts:

The first verse concerns the transgressions committed by ministers; the next verse concerns the perverted administration of rewards and punishments; the following ten verses concern the arising of evil fruits; and finally, the single verse beginning with "If a king acts contrary to the Dharma" concludes the discussion of these faults.
These are the first two [causes].

The Sūtra says: "Because of showing love and respect to evil people and punishing virtuous people, the constellations, as well as the wind and rain, all fail to proceed according to their proper seasons."
Three kinds of faults arise, and the True Dharma shall vanish; sentient beings lose their radiance and complexion, and the earth’s fertility sinks deep below.

Due to honoring the wicked and slighting the virtuous, three further faults occur: unseasonable frost and hail fall, famine and pestilence spread with suffering, and the flavor of all grains and fruits is diminished.
Within that land, sentient beings will suffer from many diseases.
The various groves of trees in the country, which once produced sweet and delicious fruits, will all diminish because of this; they will become bitter, astringent, and devoid of flavor.
Formerly there were wondrous groves and delightful places for recreation, which have suddenly withered away, causing grief and distress to all who see them.
The rice, wheat, and various fruits—their delicious flavors—gradually vanish; when eating, the heart finds no joy. How, then, can the great elements be sustained?
The radiance and complexion of sentient beings fade; their strength and vitality utterly decline. Although they consume much food, it cannot bring them satisfaction.
Among all classes of sentient beings within that realm, they possess little strength and no heroic prowess; they are incapable of accomplishing what must be done.
"The people of the land suffer many ailments, their bodies oppressed by manifold sufferings; malevolent spirits and demons spread everywhere, and rākṣasas arise in every place.
Thus, evil fruits arise below.
This section is divided into five parts:
first, one verse concerning three matters that deviate from their proper timing—namely, the stars, the wind, and the rain;
second, one verse concerning the arising of three kinds of calamities—namely, the disappearance of the True Dharma, sentient beings losing their radiance, and the depletion of the earth's fertility.

In the third section, there are two verses concerning the recurrence of three types of calamities: first, untimely frost and hail; second, the reduction of grain harvests; and third, diseases among sentient beings.

In the fourth section, there are three verses concerning the decline of external fruits, which has three aspects: one verse on all fruits lacking flavor, one verse on all forest trees withering, and one verse on food no longer providing sustenance.

In the fifth section, there are three verses concerning the regression of internal retribution, which has four aspects: one verse on physical form becoming emaciated, hungry, and feeble; one verse on the body lacking vigor and power; half a verse on being oppressed by the suffering of illness; and half a verse on the prevalence of malevolent spirits.
Sūtra: “‘If a king acts contrary to the Dharma and associates with evil persons, the three worlds will consequently suffer decline and ruin.
This concludes the fourth section, which summarizes the faults [of such conduct].
The threefold world refers to the three realms (*tridhātu*).
By means of the king’s adherence to the Dharma, humans and devas flourish; however, this is because he practices what is contrary to the Dharma.
The three realms suffer decline.
Alternatively, humans, livestock, and the hundred grains constitute the three worlds;
[in this case, decline means] epidemics among humans, loss of livestock, and the failure of the hundred grains to ripen.
As explained extensively above, the sutra states:
"Such boundless faults arise within the kingdom; all are caused by seeing wicked people and yet abandoning them rather than banishing them."
Through the protection of the devas,
one may become a king,
yet not by means of the True Dharma.
He protects the boundaries of the realm.
If a person cultivates wholesome conduct, they shall be reborn in the heavens;
if they commit evil deeds, they will surely fall into the three miserable realms after death.
If a king sees his subjects committing transgressions and permits them to continue, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas will all give rise to a heart of feverish distress.
One who does not comply with the teachings of the devas nor the words of his parents is a person who acts contrary to the Dharma; such a one is neither a true king nor a filial son.
The final five verses constitute the second major section, which establishes the violation of the True Dharma.
This section has four parts:

one verse concluding the failure to punish evil; one verse concluding the failure to cultivate goodness; one verse concluding the retribution for good and evil; and two verses concluding the violation of the teachings by non-humans.
Sūtra: “If one sees those who practice unrighteousness within one’s own kingdom, one should punish them according to the Dharma and should not abandon them.
For this reason, the hosts of devas all protect and uphold this king, because he can eliminate all unwholesome dharmas and cultivate roots of goodness.”
In this world, the King will surely receive retribution in his present life.

Because of his deeds of good and evil, he practiced equanimity and exhorted sentient beings; to demonstrate the retribution of good and evil, he has become a king of men, protected by all the devas, whom everyone follows with joy.
The following seventeen and a half verses clarify how merit accrues by relying on the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
This is divided into two parts:
first, four verses that set forth the practice of the True Dharma; second, thirteen and a half verses that provide a detailed explanation based on that outline.
Within the heading there are two parts;
these two verses indicate the punishment of evil.
There are two aspects to the punishment of evil:
The first verse praises the punishment of the wicked, and the latter verse praises the attainment of divine protection.
The following two verses set forth the exhortation to do good.
There are two aspects to this exhortation to do good:
The first verse exhorts the cultivation of virtue; the latter verse attains *bodhi*.

Sūtra: "By means of benefiting oneself and others, one should govern the kingdom according to the True Dharma (*saddharma*); when seeing those who are sycophantic and deceitful, one should punish them according to the law."
Even if one should lose their royal throne or face the loss of life, one must never practice unwholesome dharmas; seeing what is evil, one should abandon it.
Among all harms, none is more grievous than the loss of one's kingdom, for this is always caused by sycophants and flatterers; therefore, these must be punished.
If one befriends such deceitful and treacherous people, one shall surely lose one's royal throne.

Because of this, the king’s governance is ruined, like an elephant entering a flower garden; the Lord of Devas is filled with resentment, and the asuras are likewise, for he is a ruler of men yet does not govern the kingdom according to the Dharma.
"Therefore, one should, in accordance with the Dharma, punish evil persons.
This section provides an extensive explanation in two parts:
first, five and a half verses explaining the punishment of the wicked; second, eight and a half verses explaining the practice of goodness.
The explanation of the first [section] has five parts:
first, one verse on the necessity of punishing evil as soon as it is seen;
next, one verse on the abandonment of what is non-canonical.
Next, one verse clarifies the reason for the punishment;

next, one verse further reinforces the preceding point, consisting of three lines of Dharma and one line of simile; finally, one and a half verses conclude by prescribing the appropriate disciplinary measures.
Question:
How many types of evil conduct are there?
And how many kinds of punishments are there?
Answer: According to the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*, chapter four, it says: "There are five types of sentient beings who commit evil:

first, those who are of no benefit to the king; second, those who perform what is unprofitable; third, those who incite rebellion; fourth, those who engage in misconduct; and fifth, those who maintain wrong livelihood."
There are eleven kinds of actions that are detrimental to a king: first, rebellion; second, inciting others to rebel;

third, giving poison to the king; fourth, seizing the king’s means of livelihood; fifth, obstructing what ought to be done; sixth, violating the king’s wife; seventh, disobeying the king’s commands; eighth, divulging the king’s secret words; ninth, spying upon the kingdom; tenth, reviling the king; and eleventh, disparaging him.
There are ten kinds of unwholesome actions: first, mutual killing; second, mutual robbery;

third, mutual violation of each other’s wives; fourth, giving false testimony against others; fifth, deceiving others with falsehoods; sixth, destroying the friendships of others; seventh, reviling others with harsh speech; eighth, cheating others with measures and scales; ninth, mutual disparagement; and tenth, mutual arson.
"Those who are rebellious" refers to the petty kings, village chiefs, and leaders of outlying towns and settlements who do not obey the commands and decrees of the sovereign Great King.

"Those of wrong conduct" refers to those without precepts, namely those of evil livelihoods—such as butchers, hunters, and those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, dogs, geese, and ducks—who harm others and act wickedly according to their own will.
Regarding those of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): they seek various gains through unrighteous means and live by unlawful methods; each dwells in a state where they cannot support themselves.
There are three forms of punishment: first, reprimand;
second, confiscation of one's livelihood; third, imprisonment, flogging, binding, verbal abuse, and banishment.
Regarding the five types of sentient beings, they are to be disciplined according to the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior.
As for those who are rebellious, a king who practices the Dharma shall first instruct them with virtuous words in accordance with the Dharma.

If, upon hearing the king’s command, they immediately abandon their rebellious intent and request to stand before the kings as criminals, the kings shall grant them great grace and pardon their heavy offenses; they shall not diminish, seize, or expel them from the territories over which the kings rule.
Why is this? It is for the sake of making known that the king possesses three qualities: first, faith; second, benevolence; and third, great power.
By these means, those not yet subdued are brought to submission, those already subdued are prevented from acting again, and those wishing to rebel are made to dare not rise up.

That sinner shall be freed from his offense, restored to the royal throne, and the people shall live in peace; that king who rules according to the Dharma shall obtain immeasurable merit, and his good reputation shall spread far and wide.

If, upon hearing this command, they do not submit and confess their crimes, they shall be severely punished; except for taking their lives or destroying their sense organs, all their means of livelihood, lands, and subjects shall be confiscated, and they shall be banished to another place.
Why is this? It is because it prevents other sentient beings from giving rise to perversity.
This is called the practice of the Dharma-king in governing the offenses of those sentient beings who have given rise to perversity.
For sentient beings who engage in misconduct, one should only reprimand and punish them, saying:
"If you do this again, I shall inflict a heavy penalty upon you.
For sentient beings who live by wrong livelihood, one should comply with them accordingly.

The Saṃgha of the Dharma should assemble in harmony, summon [the offender] to appear before them, and take their own confession; according to the gravity of the offense, they should be dealt with according to the Dharma. If one refuses the Saṃgha’s command, does not follow the words of teachers, friends, and virtuous spiritual companions, and thereby disturbs the Saṃgha so that they cannot practice the Path—if such a king is a righteous ruler, the Saṃgha should go to him and request that the king issue a decree.
The King should summon that precept-breaking bhikṣu and, with kind words, exhort him to comply with the Sangha’s command.
If he does not comply, the two assemblies should be gathered and the matter confronted before them according to the facts.
If their offense is established, one should assist the community acting according to the Dharma in disciplining that bhikṣu.
One must not deprive him of life, nor even take away his means of subsistence; however, he may be subjected to censure or expulsion.
Great King, if two factions engage in dispute and litigation, you should adjudicate the matter in accordance with the Dharma.

If the King does not know how to do so, he should consult the great virtuous śramaṇas within the realm—those who understand the Dharma and its meaning, possess great wisdom and compassion, practice the True Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings, have a good reputation for resolving disputes, and are able to speak according to the Dharma. He should ask them about the True Dharma to determine what constitutes an offense and what does not.
Having understood this, one should act according to the Dharma to bring about their cessation.
Question:
According to the fifth chapter of the *Satyaka-sūtra*, it says: "A king who practices the Dharma, by practicing eight kinds of mental states, is able to protect sentient beings:"

First, one should contemplate all sentient beings with the thought of them being like one’s own children; second, one should contemplate sentient beings who commit evil deeds with the thought of them being like a sick child; third, one should contemplate sentient beings undergoing suffering and give rise to a mind of great compassion; fourth, one should contemplate sentient beings experiencing superior happiness and give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; fifth, one should contemplate hostile enemies and give rise to the thought of protecting them from faults; sixth, one should be able to give rise to the thought of shielding and protecting one’s own kinsmen and friends; seventh, one should be able to give rise to the thought of medicinal herbs regarding the necessities of life; eighth, one should be able to give rise to the thought of non-self regarding one’s own person.

Since he possesses these eight qualities, he is called a King who Practices the Dharma (*dharmicārī-rāja*). How then can he carry out such acts as confinement, beating, binding, and banishment? Answer:
Because he treats all sentient beings who engage in unrighteous and evil conduct with compassion, seeking to make them repent and employing skillful means to punish them, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, the third fascicle of that sutra says: "For example, when parents deal with a child who commits evil deeds, because they care for their child, they wish to cause them to repent and reform. They employ skillful means to discipline them severely, provided it does not deprive them of life or destroy their sense faculties. Other forms of discipline, such as beating or scolding, which inflict suffering according to their intent, are neither called 'abandonment of mind' nor 'an evil mind. Because their concern for the child is profound, they act to cause repentance so that the child will not do it again; thus, those parents are not said to be acting unlawfully, nor do they lose their heart of compassion."

The King who practices the Dharma is likewise: in order to cause others to abandon evil and follow what is good, and to ensure that other wicked sentient beings do not act unlawfully, he does not abandon these sentient beings with a constant state of malice, nor does he intentionally inflict suffering upon them or act with cruelty.
"To employ harsh speech and other forms of punishment against sentient beings out of a heart of compassion is not called unrighteous, nor does it constitute a loss of compassionate intent.
That sutra also says: "One who understands governance abandons a single evil person to preserve a family; one abandons a single evil family to preserve a village."
"One who does not understand governance causes people and things to lose their proper place, leading the world to resentment and litigation. Question:
"If one who practices the Dharma and acts as a king already possesses compassion, with what kind of mind should they govern and deal with those who commit evil?"

Answer: According to the third fascicle of the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*, it says: "First arouse a mind of loving-kindness; then, observe and contemplate the five dharmas with wisdom, and only thereafter should one apply the remedy."

First, relying on what is real rather than unreal; second, relying on the appropriate time rather than the inappropriate time; third, relying on meaningful content rather than meaningless content; fourth, relying on gentle speech rather than coarse or harsh speech; fifth, relying on a mind of loving-kindness rather than a mind of hatred.
This means that one should interrogate according to the law and elicit a confession, then punish based on the actual offense.
When the king has the power, he should punish the crime; when he lacks the power, he does not punish it, as this arises from an evil intention.
One should govern according to the Dharma; there is no governing other than this.
One should recognize their transgression, speak with rectitude even if it is not stable, and skillfully utter harsh words.
To reprimand in this manner—rather than failing to reprimand—is called "gentle speech."

It is not merely a matter of reprimanding and severing their transgressions; nor is it simply the removal of life or the mutilation of limbs. Rather, based on a mind of compassion, one may confine, beat, bind, scold, confiscate property, or banish them to another region—all for the purpose of inducing repentance and reform, and not out of a malicious intent to abandon them.
Question: Since a king who practices the Dharma possesses an undefiled mind of loving-kindness when punishing evildoers, why does he not take their lives or sever their limbs?
Answer:
That sutra states: "Because they possess a mind free from defilement and a mind free from malice, they are unable to give rise to such thoughts as to sever life or cut off the vital organs.
One should observe that when sentient beings reach the time of death, it arises from the transgression of their own karma; they die with a mind of hatred."
Once life has been severed, one is reborn in the evil realms, where an evil mind follows them through the long night without ceasing.
Therefore, one should not take life or sever the vital organs; for once life has been taken or the organs severed, there is no possibility of salvation thereafter.
"Because imprisonment, confinement, and verbal abuse are not permanent abandonments, the Buddha permitted them.
Furthermore, that sutra asks:

"Suppose there are ministers, officials, or prison wardens who do not consider the state's interests but seek only their own profit; or who, out of private resentment, harm public administration; or who claim to have received bribes and therefore govern unjustly."

The common people grew increasingly embroiled in mutual deception and disorder; the strong oppressed the weak, the noble the humble, the wealthy cheated the poor, and the crooked perverted the upright. The rich obtained armor [of protection], while the poor suffered humiliation; flatterers and sycophants held the administration, while the loyal and virtuous withdrew in retreat.

At times, he remained silent in court out of fear of punishment; at other times, he squandered wealth and goods for his own comfort. The common people were so impoverished and distressed that they could not be sustained; weary of suffering, they longed for chaos and paid no heed to the king’s decrees.

This arises because these officials and ministers do not practice loyalty and integrity; they deceive their superiors, bring disorder to those below, and yet presumptuously receive the king’s emoluments.
To what category among the classes of sentient beings do such persons belong?
He replied: "Great King!
He is included among those who plunder sentient beings and is subject to the highest degree of punishment."

Why is this? Because they receive the titles of royal officials and heavy stipends, yet abandon public duty for private interests and neglect the administration of the state; the arising of calamities and chaos invariably stems from this. These are the greatest traitors to the nation.
The King is a Dharma-king and must not take life; therefore, such acts are categorized among forms of robbery and subject to the highest degree of punishment.
There are many detailed categories, as fully explained in the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*.
Sūtra: “‘Transform sentient beings through goodness and do not comply with what is contrary to the Dharma. One would rather sacrifice one’s own body and life than follow unrighteous friends.
Toward both kin and non-kin, view all equally.’”
The following eight verses explain the practice of virtue, which is divided into two parts:
the first one and a half verses explain the practice of virtue, and the subsequent six and a half verses explain the benefits obtained.
Within the first part, there are again three sections:
The first half-verse concerns transforming people so they do not follow unlawful conduct;
the next half-verse concerns practicing governance so as not to follow unrighteous associates;
the final half-verse concerns rewards and punishments without discriminating between kin and non-kin.
Sūtra: “If one becomes a Dharma-king, there shall be no partiality within the realm; as a Dharma-king, he will possess a renowned reputation that is heard throughout the three realms.
The hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven will joyfully say:
‘The Dharma-king of Jambudvīpa—he is indeed our son.’”
"Transform sentient beings through goodness and govern the kingdom with the True Dharma.
Encourage the practice of the True Dharma, so that they shall be born in my palace.
Because of the King’s transformation through the True Dharma, the devas, the sons of the devas, and the hosts of asuras always attained joy in their hearts.
The hosts of devas all rejoice, together protecting the king of men.

The myriad stars move according to their stations; the sun and moon do not deviate from their courses. Gentle breezes always accord with the seasons, and sweet rain falls in due time. Crops and fruits all ripen well, and among the people there is no hunger or famine.
"All the hosts of devas shall fill their own palaces.
Thus ends the explanation of the benefits obtained, which consists of six parts;
the first verse describes the benefit of obtaining a name that is widely renowned.
The next verse provides the benefit of becoming a celestial king;
the next verse provides the benefit of being reborn in heaven;
and the next one and a half verses provide the benefit of being joyfully protected by the devas.
The next two verses concern the protection of the state and its benefits, which are further divided into four parts:

one half-verse on the benefit of the constellations following their proper courses; one half-verse on the benefit of wind being harmonious and rain being timely; one half-verse on the benefit of the people being abundant and joyful; and one half-verse on the benefit of being able to protect the various devas, because it causes the hosts of devas to be constantly full.
Question:
A king who is able to practice virtue gains the protection of the devas; how then can he benefit from their protection? Answer:

The King practiced the True Dharma and extensively propagated the Buddha’s teachings; as the country was peaceful and the people lived in security, he constantly encouraged them to cultivate goodness, so that many were reborn in the heavens.
Furthermore, he spread the Buddha-dharma, and the devas heard it and gained benefit.
Therefore, the *Satyaka-sūtra* states: "A king who practices the Dharma is protected by immeasurable devas. How do these devas protect him?

Because the king who practices the Dharma is able to provide the pure food of the True Dharma to the devas—namely, by expounding for them the nectar-like Dharma-gates of the Tathāgata’s true teaching, such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and the ten paths of wholesome action—thereby enabling them to be free from the sufferings of the various evil realms; it is in this way that they protect him."

Therefore, a king who acts according to the Dharma is able to accumulate immeasurable merit within his own person to benefit the present, and will further be able to gather all fruits of goodness in the future.

As it is said below: "For this reason, you, O King of Men, should disregard your own body to propagate the True Dharma; you ought to revere the Jewel of the Dharma, for by this, the multitude shall find peace and happiness."
The "Chapter on the Four Kings Protecting the Nation" also explains this in detail.

The Sūtra says: "Therefore, you, O King of Men, should disregard your own person to propagate the True Dharma; you ought to revere the Jewel of the Dharma, for by this, the multitude shall find peace and happiness."
One should always draw near to the True Dharma, adorning oneself with merit; one’s retinue will always be joyful, and one will be able to remain far removed from all evils.

By transforming sentient beings through the Dharma, one constantly enables them to attain peace and security, causing all those people to practice the ten wholesome deeds; thus the entire land will always be abundant and happy, and the kingdom will enjoy tranquility.
“A king who transforms people through the Dharma and skillfully disciplines their evil conduct shall obtain a good reputation and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
Within the exposition of the luminous True Dharma there are three parts; the above constitutes the second section, which extensively presents the True Discourse.
Next, the third section, "Exhortation to Rely on Training," is divided into three parts:
first, a single verse exhorting the propagation of the Dharma for the benefit of others;
second, half a verse exhorting the pursuit of the Dharma for one's own benefit.
The final three verses clarify its benefits, which are fourfold:

the first half-verse clarifies that one’s retinue is free from wrongdoing; the next half-verse clarifies the physical happiness of sentient beings; the next verse clarifies the abundance of the land and the well-being of the people; and the final verse clarifies the attainment of a good reputation.

Sūtra: At that time, all the kings of men upon the great earth and the entire great assembly, having heard the Buddha expound these essential methods for governing a kingdom used by ancient kings, attained what they had never experienced before; they were all greatly rejoiced, and with faith and acceptance, they put them into practice.
